title: 7 Best Home Theater Amplifiers in 2026: Add Real Power
metaDescription: 7 amps for receiver pre-outs: the Outlaw Audio 5000x (5 x 120 W into 8 ohms) is best for most, the 7000x for 7 channels, Monolith 5x200 for tough speakers.
h1: The 7 Best Home Theater Amplifiers in 2026
keywords: best 5 channel amplifier for home theater
best 2 channel amp for home theater
best external amplifier for home theater
best amp for home theater and music
best class d amplifier for home theater
intro:
Adding a power amp will not make your system much louder; it gives your speakers headroom and lets your receiver run cooler. It only works if your receiver has pre-outs. Here are the 7 amps that make sense.

The best home theater amplifier for most AV receiver owners is the **[Outlaw Audio 5000x](/gear/outlaw-audio-5000x/)**: a five-channel power amp rated at **120 W per channel into 8 ohms (180 W into 4 ohms)**, which takes the speakers that carry most of a movie (front left, center, right and both surrounds) off your receiver's amp and frees its power supply for the heights. This guide is for people who already own an AVR with pre-outs, or are planning one, and want more headroom, more channels, or a better stereo setup for music.

An external amp doesn't replace a receiver; it adds to it. We rank each pick by what problem it solves: more power for the ear-level speakers, more channels for big Atmos layouts, or a dedicated stereo amp for music. If you need seven channels at once, the **[Outlaw Audio 7000x](/gear/outlaw-audio-7000x/)** is rated at 130 W per channel with all seven driven.
quickAnswer: The Outlaw Audio 5000x is the best home theater amplifier for most people: five channels at 120 W each into 8 ohms to power your front left, center, right and surround speakers from your receiver's pre-outs. For a full seven-channel upgrade, the Outlaw Audio 7000x delivers 130 W per channel with all channels driven, and the Monolith 5x200 offers 200 W per channel for big rooms. For music, a stereo integrated amp like the Yamaha A-S501 is a better fit.
picksHeading: The best amplifiers for home theater

picks.body:
In a 5.1 movie mix, the **center carries almost all the dialogue**, the front left and right carry most of the music and effects, and the two surrounds handle ambience and pans. Those five ear-level speakers do nearly all the work, so moving them to a dedicated amp is the most complete single upgrade for a receiver-based system. The 5000x does exactly that.

Outlaw rates it at **120 W per channel into 8 ohms and 180 W into 4 ohms, 20 Hz–20 kHz, under 0.02% THD**. It has **balanced XLR and RCA inputs**, a **12 V trigger** so it wakes with your receiver, and separate rectification and a protection relay for each channel. The listing doesn't say how many channels are driven for that rating, so read it as a per-channel figure rather than an all-channels guarantee.

The maths: an 88 dB [sensitivity](/glossary/speaker-sensitivity/) center at a 3-meter seat gives about 78.5 dB from 1 W. At 120 W you add 20.8 dB for **about 99 dB** of clean dialogue, while the receiver's supply is left to power only the heights.

The trade-off: you need a receiver with **pre-outs for five channels**. Entry models like the [Denon AVR-S770H](/gear/denon-avr-s770h/) don't have them; the [Denon AVR-X3800H](/gear/denon-avr-x3800h/) and [Marantz Cinema 50](/gear/marantz-cinema-50/) do. Compared with the seven-channel [Outlaw Audio 7000x](/gear/outlaw-audio-7000x/), you give up two channels and 10 W per channel but spend less, which suits most 5.1 and 5.1.4 rooms.

If you run a 7.1 or 7.1.4 system, the 7000x takes **every ear-level speaker** off your receiver. Outlaw rates it at **130 W per channel into 8 ohms and 200 W into 4 ohms, with all seven channels driven**, 20 Hz–20 kHz at under 0.03% THD. That all-channels figure is the one most receivers never publish: seven channels × 130 W = **910 W** of rated output with everything working.

Like the 5000x, it has **balanced XLR and RCA inputs**, a **12 V trigger**, per-channel rectification and protection relays, a 111 dBA signal-to-noise rating and a **five-year warranty**, all in the same 17-inch-wide, 16.75-inch-deep chassis.

Where it fits: a 7.1.4 layout has 11 speakers. The 7000x powers the seven ear-level channels, and a nine-channel receiver such as the [Denon AVR-X3800H](/gear/denon-avr-x3800h/) only has to drive the four heights. With an 87 dB speaker at a 3-meter seat, 130 W gives about **98.5 dB** per channel, plenty for most medium and large rooms once a subwoofer takes the bass.

The trade-off: per channel, it's only about 0.9 dB louder than a receiver channel rated at 105 W, so the gain is mostly headroom on loud scenes and a lighter load on the receiver's supply. Against the [Monolith 5x200](/gear/monolith-5x200/), you trade 1.9 dB per channel for two extra channels in a lower price band. It's the best 7 channel home theater amplifier for the money.

picks.award: Best for Large Rooms and Inefficient Speakers
picks.body:
If your speakers are inefficient or your seats sit far back, the Monolith 5x200 is the heavyweight choice. Monoprice rates it at **200 W per channel into 8 ohms with all five channels driven, 20 Hz–20 kHz**, from a **Class AB** design with **two toroidal transformers**, no current limiting in the signal path and a signal-to-noise ratio above **120 dB**. Each channel takes **balanced XLR or RCA**.

The maths: against the [Outlaw Audio 5000x](/gear/outlaw-audio-5000x/) at 120 W, 10 × log10(200 ÷ 120) = **2.2 dB** more headroom per channel. With an 87 dB speaker at a 3-meter seat, 200 W reaches about **100.5 dB**, close to reference level once a subwoofer handles the bass. With 85 dB speakers in a bigger room, those extra 2 dB are the difference between clean peaks and a receiver running out of steam.

In a 7.1.4 build, put the front three and side surrounds on the Monolith and let a nine-channel receiver power the rear surrounds and four heights.

The trade-offs are heat, space and price. Class AB runs warm, so leave open space above it, and it sits in a higher price band than both Outlaw amps while offering two fewer channels than the 7000x. Who it suits: dedicated theaters, large rooms and low-sensitivity speakers. In an ordinary living room with efficient speakers, the 5000x does the same job for less.

For many systems, the front left and right speakers are also the music speakers, and they deserve a dedicated amp. The MM7025 is a **two-channel power amplifier** rated at **140 W per channel into 8 ohms and 170 W into 6 ohms**, with an **oversized EI-core power transformer**, Marantz's current-feedback design and **balanced XLR or RCA inputs** on each channel. Auto-standby and remote power control let it wake with the system.

It solves two problems. First, it gives large towers such as the [Polk Reserve R700](/gear/polk-reserve-r700/) or [KEF R7 Meta](/gear/kef-r7-meta/) their own power supply. Second, it completes a big Atmos layout: a 7.1.4 system has 11 speakers, a nine-channel receiver like the [Marantz Cinema 50](/gear/marantz-cinema-50/) powers nine, and the MM7025 drives the remaining two, usually the front pair.

The maths: against a receiver channel rated at 105 W, 10 × log10(140 ÷ 105) = **1.25 dB** more headroom. The bigger gain is that the receiver now feeds nine channels instead of eleven. With 86 dB towers at 3.5 meters, 140 W gives about **96.5 dB** at the seat.

The trade-off: two channels only, so your center stays on the receiver's amp, and you pay more per channel than with the Outlaw amps. For dialogue-heavy viewing, the [Outlaw Audio 5000x](/gear/outlaw-audio-5000x/) is the more balanced upgrade. It's the best 2 channel amp for home theater when music matters as much as movies.

picks.award: Best Budget Amp for Height Channels
picks.body:
The Fosi Audio V3 is a compact **Class D stereo amplifier** built around Texas Instruments' **TPA3255** chip. It's small enough to sit beside a receiver and costs a fraction of the other power amps here, which makes it a smart, cheap way to add **two extra channels**.

The obvious use is Atmos heights. If your receiver processes more channels than it amplifies (such as the [Denon AVR-X3800H](/gear/denon-avr-x3800h/), which amplifies nine and processes eleven), the V3 can power the extra pair of height speakers to reach **7.1.4**. Height speakers are typically small and handle little bass, so they don't need a big Class AB amp.

Fosi's headline power figures are quoted into 4 ohms with a high-voltage power supply; into typical 8-ohm height speakers, expect considerably less. That's still plenty for ceiling speakers like the [Polk RC80i](/gear/polk-rc80i/) or elevation modules like the [Klipsch R-41SA](/gear/klipsch-r-41sa/).

The trade-offs: check whether it can switch on automatically with your receiver (otherwise use a switched outlet), its volume knob needs setting once and leaving, and long-term durability of budget Class D amps varies more than established brands. Don't use it to power demanding front towers. As the best budget amplifier for home theater add-on channels, though, it's hard to beat.

picks.award: Best Integrated Amp for Music and TV
picks.body:
Not everyone needs surround sound. If you want a great **2.1 system** for music that also handles the TV, an integrated amplifier is simpler than a receiver, and the Yamaha A-S501 is one of the most sensible choices. Yamaha rates it at **85 W per channel into 8 ohms (20 Hz–20 kHz)**, and it includes **optical and coaxial digital inputs** with a built-in DAC, a **phono stage** for turntables and a **subwoofer output** for 2.1.

Connect your TV's optical output to the A-S501, add a pair of [bookshelf speakers](/best-bookshelf-speakers-for-home-theater/) and a [subwoofer](/best-subwoofer-for-home-theater/), and you have a stereo TV system that will outperform many soundbars with music. **Pure Direct** mode bypasses tone controls for the cleanest signal path.

The trade-off: no HDMI, no surround decoding and no home theater bypass input. Optical carries Dolby Digital and PCM stereo but not lossless formats; the TV downmixes to two channels. The sub output is a simple filtered feed, without the bass management and room correction an AVR provides.

Who it suits: music-first listeners, apartments and second rooms. If you later want 5.1, a receiver like the [Yamaha RX-V4A](/gear/yamaha-rx-v4a/) is the next step, and the A-S501 can move to a bedroom or office.

The Denon PMA-600NE is the budget version of the same idea: a stereo integrated amp with enough connectivity to double as a TV amp. Denon rates it at **45 W per channel into 8 ohms** and **70 W into 4 ohms**, and it includes a built-in DAC with **optical and coaxial inputs**, **Bluetooth** and a **moving-magnet phono stage**.

Forty-five watts sounds small, but do the maths. With 88 dB-sensitive bookshelf speakers at 2.5 meters, 1 W gives about 80 dB at the seat (2.5 m costs about 8 dB). At 45 W you add 16.5 dB for **roughly 96 dB per speaker**, which is loud for a small living room or bedroom. Efficient speakers like the [Klipsch R-50M](/gear/klipsch-r-50m/) make it even more comfortable.

The trade-off compared with the [Yamaha A-S501](/gear/yamaha-a-s501/): less power and no dedicated subwoofer output, so adding a sub means using its speaker-level inputs (if your sub has them) or choosing a sub with a high-level input like the [REL T/5x](/gear/rel-t5x/). It also has no HDMI or surround decoding.

Who it suits: a second system, a desk setup or a first stereo for music and TV on a small budget. If you want the best amp for home theater and music in one box, a receiver still wins; this is the pick if music comes first.

sections.heading: Amplifier vs Receiver: Which Do You Need?
sections.body:
A **receiver** (AVR) is a surround processor, multichannel amplifier, HDMI switcher, room-correction engine and streamer in one box. A **power amplifier** does one job: it takes a line-level signal and makes it powerful enough to drive speakers. An **integrated amplifier** adds a volume control, source switching and sometimes a DAC, but usually has no surround decoding or HDMI.

So which is best for home theater? For surround sound, you need a receiver or a separate processor either way. An external amp is an **addition**, and it makes sense in four cases:

- **Your speakers are hard to drive** (low sensitivity or 4-ohm loads) and the receiver runs out of headroom.
- **Your room is large**, so you sit far from the speakers and lose level with distance.
- **You want more channels** than the receiver amplifies, such as going from 5.1.4 to 7.1.4.
- **You want a better stereo amp** for the front pair because they double as music speakers.

If none of those apply, spend the money on [better speakers](/best-home-theater-speakers/) or a [second subwoofer](/best-subwoofer-for-home-theater/) instead; both make a bigger audible difference.

sections.heading: What to Look For in a Home Theater Power Amp
sections.body:
**Power rating with all channels driven.** The most useful number for a multichannel amp is power with all channels driven at 8 ohms across 20 Hz–20 kHz. The [Outlaw Audio 7000x](/gear/outlaw-audio-7000x/) and [Monolith 5x200](/gear/monolith-5x200/) quote their ratings this way. The [Outlaw Audio 5000x](/gear/outlaw-audio-5000x/) listing gives 120 W per channel without saying how many channels are driven, so read it as a per-channel figure.

**Headroom in decibels, not watts.** Doubling power adds 3 dB. Going from a receiver's 100 W to a 200 W amp adds 3 dB of headroom: noticeable at high volume, invisible at normal levels.

**Class AB vs Class D.** Class AB amps (like the Monolith 5x200 and both integrated amps here) are heavy and run warm but have a long track record. Class D amps (like the [Fosi Audio V3](/gear/fosi-audio-v3/)) are compact and efficient; modern designs measure very well. Either is fine for home theater; choose based on space, heat and budget.

**Inputs.** Receivers' pre-outs are almost always RCA. All four power amps here also take balanced XLR, but XLR matters only if you use a processor with XLR outputs or long cable runs.

**Trigger and auto-on.** A 12 V trigger input lets the receiver turn the amp on and off. Without it, use auto signal sensing or a switched outlet.

**Impedance.** If your speakers dip to 4 ohms, look for an amp rated into 4 ohms, ideally with close to double the 8-ohm figure. See [impedance](/glossary/impedance/).

sections.heading: How We Chose the Best Home Theater Amplifier Picks
sections.body:
These picks are based on manufacturer specs, the maths of speaker sensitivity and distance, independent measurements where they're widely published, and owner-reported reliability.

We ranked by the problem each amp solves for a home theater owner:

1. **Impact per dollar.** The five ear-level channels (front three plus surrounds) carry nearly all of a movie mix, so the [Outlaw Audio 5000x](/gear/outlaw-audio-5000x/) beat the seven-channel [Outlaw Audio 7000x](/gear/outlaw-audio-7000x/) for most people: it costs less, and most receivers can comfortably power the heights themselves.
2. **Honest power.** All-channels-driven ratings were weighted above two-channel or 4-ohm figures, and we say so where a listing doesn't state how many channels are driven.
3. **Fit with real receivers.** Every multichannel pick works with standard RCA pre-outs found on mid-range and premium AVRs.
4. **Practicality.** Weight, heat, size and turn-on behavior matter when the amp shares a rack with a receiver.
5. **Track record.** Brands with long reliability histories and good service ranked higher.

sections.heading: How Many Amplifier Channels Do You Need?
sections.body:
Match the amp to the job:

| Goal | Channels to add | Pick |
|---|---|---|
| More power for the five ear-level speakers of a 5.1 or 5.1.4 system | 5 | [Outlaw Audio 5000x](/gear/outlaw-audio-5000x/) |
| The same job in a large room or with inefficient speakers | 5 | [Monolith 5x200](/gear/monolith-5x200/) |
| Every ear-level speaker in a 7.1 or 7.1.4 room | 7 | [Outlaw Audio 7000x](/gear/outlaw-audio-7000x/) |
| Better music from the front pair, or the last two channels of a 7.1.4 build | 2 (L/R) | [Marantz MM7025](/gear/marantz-mm7025/) |
| Extra Atmos heights on a budget (5.1.4 to 7.1.4) | 2 | [Fosi Audio V3](/gear/fosi-audio-v3/) |
| Front left, center and right only | 3 | Use a five-channel amp and leave two channels spare |

**Best 3 channel amp for home theater?** Dedicated three-channel amps for the front stage exist, but none made our list. A five-channel amp like the 5000x covers the same three speakers plus the surrounds, and if you only want L/C/R amplified today, the two spare channels are ready when your receiver starts to struggle with the surrounds.

Do the channel count before you buy: 7.1.4 is 7 + 4 = **11 speakers**. A nine-channel receiver plus a 2-channel amp covers it; so does a 7-channel amp with the receiver powering the four heights.

When you add an external amp, check that your receiver can **reassign** its freed-up internal channels. Many Denon, Marantz and Onkyo models can use them for heights or a second zone.

sections.heading: Does Your Receiver Have Pre-Outs?
sections.body:
Pre-outs are line-level RCA outputs, one per channel, that feed an external amplifier. Without them, a power amp can't connect to your receiver in a home theater.

- **Entry receivers** usually have only subwoofer pre-outs and sometimes a zone 2 output. The [Denon AVR-S770H](/gear/denon-avr-s770h/) and [Yamaha RX-V4A](/gear/yamaha-rx-v4a/) aren't built for external amps on the main channels.
- **Enthusiast receivers** have pre-outs for every processed channel. The [Denon AVR-X3800H](/gear/denon-avr-x3800h/) and [Marantz Cinema 50](/gear/marantz-cinema-50/) offer full 11.4 pre-outs.

Before buying an amp, look at the receiver's back panel or manual for a "PRE OUT" block and count the channels. If your receiver lacks them, the upgrade path is a better receiver, not an amp. Our [receiver guide](/best-home-theater-receiver/) lists which picks are expandable.

sections.heading: Integrated Amps and Home Theater Bypass
sections.body:
A **home theater bypass** (also called "HT bypass," "main in" or "unity gain") input on a stereo integrated amp lets your receiver control volume for movies while the integrated amp powers the front pair. It's how many people run one set of front speakers for both a high-end stereo and a surround system.

The two integrated amps here, the [Yamaha A-S501](/gear/yamaha-a-s501/) and [Denon PMA-600NE](/gear/denon-pma-600ne/), **don't have a dedicated bypass input**. You can still feed them from a receiver's pre-outs, but you'll need to set the integrated amp's volume to the same position every time you watch a movie, or levels will be wrong after calibration. That's workable but fiddly.

Our recommendation: if you want one front pair for both stereo and surround, use a **power amp** like the [Marantz MM7025](/gear/marantz-mm7025/) on the receiver's front pre-outs and use the receiver's stereo or direct mode for music. Keep integrated amps for dedicated 2.0 or 2.1 systems.

sections.heading: Who Should Buy an External Amp, and Who Can Skip It
sections.body:
**Buy an amp if:** your receiver has pre-outs and your speakers are below 86 dB sensitive, your seats are more than about 4 meters from the screen, you want 7.1.4 from an 11-channel receiver, or you want a dedicated stereo amp for music.

**Skip it if:** your receiver lacks pre-outs, your speakers are efficient (88 dB or higher) in a normal living room, or you rarely listen loud. You'll get more from [room correction](/glossary/room-correction/), better speaker placement or a second subwoofer. Read our [home theater setup guide](/home-theater-setup-guide/) before spending on power you won't use.

mistakes.title: Buying an amp for a receiver without pre-outs
mistakes.body: Without per-channel pre-outs, a power amp has nothing to connect to. Check the receiver's back panel first.

mistakes.title: Expecting a big jump in loudness
mistakes.body: Doubling power adds only 3 dB. An amp buys headroom and lower distortion at high volume, not a dramatically louder system at normal levels.

mistakes.title: Ignoring all-channels-driven ratings
mistakes.body: Receivers and amps quoted two channels driven can deliver much less with seven working. Compare all-channels ratings for multichannel amps.

mistakes.title: Forgetting to recalibrate
mistakes.body: An external amp changes gain. Rerun Audyssey, YPAO or Dirac after connecting it so levels and distances are right.

mistakes.title: Putting a heavy Class AB amp in a closed cabinet
mistakes.body: Big amps run warm. Give them open space above and behind, or add a quiet fan, especially when stacked near a receiver.

faqs.q: Do I need an amplifier for my home theater?
faqs.a: Most people don't. A modern receiver powers typical 6–8 ohm speakers well in a normal living room. You need an external amplifier if your speakers are inefficient or 4-ohm, your room is large, you want more channels than the receiver amplifies, or you want better stereo performance from the front pair.

faqs.q: Is an amplifier better than a receiver for home theater?
faqs.a: They do different jobs. A receiver decodes surround sound, switches HDMI and corrects the room; an amplifier only adds power. For home theater, you need a receiver or processor regardless. An amp can make it better by taking on the hardest-working channels, but it can't replace it.

faqs.q: What is the best 5-channel amp for home theater?
faqs.a: The Outlaw Audio 5000x is the best 5-channel amp for home theater for most people. It's rated at 120 W per channel into 8 ohms and 180 W into 4 ohms, enough for the front left, center, right and two surrounds, which carry nearly all of a 5.1 mix. For big rooms and inefficient speakers, the Monolith 5x200 steps up to 200 W per channel with all channels driven.

faqs.q: What is the best 7-channel home theater amplifier?
faqs.a: The Outlaw Audio 7000x is the best 7-channel home theater amplifier, rated at 130 W per channel into 8 ohms and 200 W into 4 ohms with all seven channels driven, plus XLR inputs and a 12 V trigger. If you only need five channels and want more power for each, the Monolith 5x200 delivers 200 W per channel into 8 ohms.

faqs.q: How many watts do I need for home theater?
faqs.a: Work it out from speaker sensitivity and seat distance. An 87 dB speaker at 3 m gives about 77.5 dB from 1 W; 100 W adds 20 dB for 97.5 dB. That's loud for most rooms. Reaching 105 dB peaks with that speaker needs several hundred watts, which is where external amps help.

faqs.q: Is Class D good for home theater?
faqs.a: Yes. Modern Class D amplifiers measure very well, run cool and fit in small spaces, which suits height channels and crowded racks. Class AB amps are heavier and warmer but have a long track record. For home theater, design quality and honest ratings matter more than class.

faqs.q: Can I use a stereo amp with an AV receiver?
faqs.a: Yes, if the receiver has front left and right pre-outs. Connect them to a stereo power amp's inputs and the amp drives your front speakers while the receiver powers the rest. An integrated amp without a home theater bypass input also works, but you must set its volume to the same position each time.

bottomLine:
The **Outlaw Audio 5000x** is the best home theater amplifier for most people because it powers the five ear-level speakers that carry most of a movie, at 120 W per channel into 8 ohms. Go for the **Outlaw Audio 7000x** to take all seven ear-level channels off your receiver at 130 W each with all channels driven, or the **Monolith 5x200** for 200 W per channel in a big room with inefficient speakers. The **Marantz MM7025** is the music-first stereo amp for front towers or the last two channels of a 7.1.4 build, and the **Fosi Audio V3** is a cheap way to add Atmos heights. For 2.1 music-and-TV systems, the **Yamaha A-S501** and **Denon PMA-600NE** are simpler than a receiver.

Driving demanding flagship towers? [Our high-end speaker picks](/best-high-end-home-theater-speakers/) include the 4-ohm amp maths.
